source: ICAR Technical Bulletin No. 45 — Integrated Pest Management for Field Crops
text: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) is the recommended approach for sustainable agriculture in India. The IPM strategy follows a hierarchical approach: Step 1: Cultural practices — deep summer ploughing exposes soil-borne pests to sun, destroying 60-70% of pupae. Crop rotation with non-host crops breaks pest cycles. Step 2: Monitoring — scout fields weekly, checking leaf undersides, stems, and soil surface. Use pheromone traps (5/hectare) for bollworm, fruit fly. Yellow sticky traps (20/hectare) for whitefly, aphids, thrips. Light traps for stem borers. Step 3: Biological control — release Trichogramma wasps (1.5 lakh/hectare) for bollworm. Use Beauveria bassiana (2kg/hectare) for white grub. NPV (Nuclear Polyhedrosis Virus) 250 LE/hectare for Helicoverpa. Step 4: Botanical pesticides — Neem-based (Azadirachtin 0.03%) as first chemical line. Neem seed kernel extract 5% for sucking pests. Step 5: Chemical control only when Economic Threshold Level (ETL) is crossed. For wheat: Aphid ETL is 5 aphids per ear head. For cotton: Bollworm ETL is 1 larva per plant or 5% fruiting body damage. For soybean: Girdle beetle — 3 grubs per meter row. Always rotate pesticide chemical groups to prevent resistance. Banned pesticides: NEVER use DDT, endosulfan, monocrotophos, methyl parathion, phorate — banned under the Insecticides Act, 1968.

source: ICAR-IIWBR — Pest Management for Wheat in Central India
text: Major wheat pests in Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, and Rajasthan: 1. Aphids (Sitobion avenae, Rhopalosiphum padi): Appear during ear-head stage (February-March). Colonies on leaves and ear heads. Secrete honeydew causing sooty mould. ETL: 5 aphids per ear head or 10-15% plant infestation. Control: Spray Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ 0.5ml/litre or Thiamethoxam 25 WG @ 0.3g/litre. Avoid spraying during flowering (bee safety). 2. Leaf Rust (Puccinia triticina): Most damaging disease. Brown-orange pustules on leaf surface. Can reduce yield by 10-30%. Control: Spray Propiconazole 25 EC @ 0.1% at first appearance. Resistant varieties: HD-2967, HD-3086, DBW-187. 3. Yellow Rust (Puccinia striiformis): Yellow-orange stripes along leaf veins. More severe in cooler regions. Spray Propiconazole or Tebuconazole 25.9 EC @ 0.1%. 4. Karnal Bunt (Tilletia indica): Black powdery mass in grains with fishy smell. Seed treatment with Vitavax 75 WP @ 2.5g/kg prevents 80% incidence. 5. Termites: Major problem in light soils. Apply Chlorpyrifos 20 EC @ 5L/hectare in irrigation water. Treat seed with Fipronil 5 SC @ 6ml/kg. 6. Pink Stem Borer (Sesamia inferens): Install light traps in November. Spray Cartap hydrochloride 50 SP @ 1kg/hectare. Preventive measures: Use certified treated seed. Practice crop rotation with pulses. Avoid late sowing (after December 15). Remove crop residue after harvest.

source: National Programme for Organic Production (NPOP) — APEDA Guidelines
text: Organic farming certification and practices under NPOP (National Programme for Organic Production): Conversion Period: Minimum 2 years for annual crops, 3 years for perennial crops before produce can be sold as 'organic'. During conversion, follow all organic practices but label as 'In-Conversion'. Key organic inputs: 1. Jeevamrutha (microbial culture): Mix 200L water + 10kg fresh cow dung + 10L cow urine + 2kg jaggery + 2kg pulse flour + handful of forest soil in a barrel. Stir twice daily, ferment 48 hours. Apply 500L/acre every 15 days. Activates soil microbiome, provides growth hormones. 2. Panchagavya: Cow dung 7kg + cow urine 3L + milk 2L + curd 2L + ghee 1L + sugarcane juice 3L + tender coconut water 3L + ripened banana 12 nos. Ferment 21 days stirring twice daily. Use as 3% foliar spray. 3. Vermicompost: Use Eisenia foetida (red wiggler worms). Bedding: half-decomposed crop residue + cow dung. Harvest after 60-90 days. Apply 2-3 tonnes/hectare. Rich in NPK, humic acid, beneficial microbes. 4. Green manuring: Dhaincha (Sesbania aculeata) — sow at 25kg/ha, incorporate at 45 days. Fixes 60-80 kg nitrogen/hectare. Sunhemp (Crotalaria juncea) — fixes 80-100 kg N/ha. 5. Bio-fertilizers: Rhizobium for legumes, Azotobacter for cereals, PSB (Phosphate Solubilizing Bacteria) for phosphorus mobilization. Certification: Apply through APEDA-accredited agencies (INDOCERT, OneCert, Lacon Quality). Cost: Rs 5,000-15,000/year for individual farmers. Group certification (PGS — Participatory Guarantee System) through Regional Councils costs Rs 500-1,000/farmer. Premium: Organic produce fetches 20-40% premium in domestic market, 50-100% in export. Register on Jaivik Kheti portal (jaivikkheti.in) for direct marketing.

source: IARI Extension Bulletin — Micro-Irrigation for Indian Agriculture
text: Drip irrigation system design and management for Indian farms: Water savings: 30-50% compared to flood irrigation. Yield increase: 20-30% due to uniform water and nutrient application. System components: Water source (well/canal) → Pump (HP based on area) → Sand filter + disc filter → Mainline (PVC 63-75mm) → Sub-mainline (PVC 40-50mm) → Laterals (LDPE 12mm for vegetables, 16mm for row crops) → Drippers (inline or online, 2/4/8 LPH). Crop-specific design: Cotton — paired row 150cm × 45cm, dripper spacing 40cm, 4 LPH. Sugarcane — single row 150cm, dripper 60cm spacing, 4 LPH. Vegetables — raised bed, lateral spacing 60cm, dripper 30cm, 2 LPH. Banana — ring system, 8 LPH dripper, 2 per plant. Fertigation schedule: Use water-soluble fertilizers only. NPK 19:19:19 for vegetative stage, 13:0:45 for fruit/grain development, Calcium Nitrate for quality. Inject through venturi injector (low cost) or dosing pump (precise). NEVER mix calcium fertilizers with sulphate-based ones — causes precipitation and clogging. Maintenance: Daily — check pressure (1.0-1.5 kg/cm²), look for leaks. Weekly — clean filters (backwash sand filter, manually clean disc). Monthly — flush lateral ends for 2-3 minutes. Seasonally — acid treatment (HCl 0.5%) for emitter cleaning. Government subsidy under PMKSY-PDMC: 55% for general category farmers, 70% for SC/ST and small/marginal farmers (<2 hectares). Apply through state horticulture department or mahadbt.maharashtra.gov.in (Maharashtra). Required documents: 7/12 extract, Aadhaar, bank passbook, soil/water test report.

source: Soil Health Card Scheme — Department of Agriculture & Farmers' Welfare
text: Soil Health Card (SHC) scheme provides free soil testing and nutrient management recommendations to all farmers. How to get tested: Submit soil samples to nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK), agricultural university soil lab, or state soil testing lab. Collect samples: Take 10-15 sub-samples from a field in V-pattern at 15cm depth. Mix, take 500g, air-dry, label with GPS coordinates. Testing frequency: Once every 2 crop cycles (2-3 years). Parameters tested: Primary — pH, Electrical Conductivity (EC), Organic Carbon (OC). Macronutrients — Available Nitrogen (N), Phosphorus (P₂O₅), Potassium (K₂O). Secondary — Sulphur (S). Micronutrients — Zinc (Zn), Boron (B), Iron (Fe), Manganese (Mn), Copper (Cu). Ideal ranges for Maharashtra black soil (Vertisol): pH 7.0-8.0, EC < 1.0 dS/m, OC > 0.5% (target >0.75%), N > 280 kg/ha, P > 25 kg/ha, K > 280 kg/ha, S > 10 ppm, Zn > 0.6 ppm. For Maharashtra red soil (Alfisol): pH 5.5-7.0, OC > 0.4%, N > 200 kg/ha. Improving soil health: 1. Organic carbon — apply FYM 5-10 tonnes/ha, vermicompost 2-3 tonnes/ha, incorporate crop residue (don't burn). 2. Nitrogen — crop rotation with legumes (gram, moong, tur) fixes 40-100 kg N/ha naturally. Save Rs 2,000-4,000/ha on urea. 3. Phosphorus — apply Single Super Phosphate (SSP) which also provides sulphur and calcium. Use PSB inoculation. 4. Micronutrients — Zinc sulphate 25 kg/ha for deficient soils. Borax 10 kg/ha for mustard, sunflower. 5. Problem soils — Saline soil: apply gypsum, grow salt-tolerant varieties. Acidic soil: apply lime 2-4 tonnes/ha. Waterlogged: improve drainage, grow rice.

source: CWRDM & ICAR — Water Management in Rainfed Agriculture
text: Water management strategies for rainfed and irrigated agriculture in Maharashtra: Rainwater harvesting: Farm ponds (Jal Shakti) — excavate 30m × 30m × 3m lined pond to store 27 lakh litres. Sufficient to provide 2 supplemental irrigations to 2 hectares of soybean/cotton. Cost: Rs 1.5-3 lakh. Subsidy under MGNREGA (90 person-days labour) and PMKSY Watershed component. Maharashtra Magel Tyala Shet Tale Yojana provides up to Rs 50,000 subsidy. Check dams and percolation tanks for village-level recharge. Mulching: Reduces evaporation by 25-30%, moderates soil temperature. Crop residue mulch — free, improves soil organic matter. Black plastic mulch — Rs 8,000/ha, excellent for vegetables and sugarcane. Silver mulch — repels whitefly (good for tomato, chilli). Crop water requirements (seasonal totals in mm): Wheat 400-500mm (5 irrigations), Cotton 600-800mm, Sugarcane 1500-2000mm, Soybean 400-500mm (rainfed OK), Onion 500-600mm, Rice 1200-1400mm, Jowar 400-500mm. Critical irrigation stages (never miss these): Wheat — CRI (21 days), flowering (80 days), grain filling (100 days). Cotton — square formation, flowering, boll development. Sugarcane — tillering, grand growth (July-September). Rice — transplanting, tillering, flowering. Deficit irrigation: Apply 80% of crop water requirement during vegetative stage, full water at critical stages. Saves 20% water with only 5-8% yield penalty. Ideal for limited water areas. Soil moisture monitoring: Tensiometer (Rs 500-1000) — irrigate when reading > 40 centibars for heavy soils, > 25 for light soils. Digital sensors available through KVK demonstrations.

source: PM-KISAN Official Guidelines — Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers' Welfare
text: Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM-KISAN) — India's largest direct benefit transfer scheme for farmers. Benefits: Rs 6,000 per year transferred in 3 equal instalments of Rs 2,000 each. Schedule: Instalment 1 (April-July), Instalment 2 (August-November), Instalment 3 (December-March). Payment: Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) into Aadhaar-linked bank account. eKYC mandatory since 2022 — complete through PM-KISAN portal or via OTP on mobile. Eligibility: All land-holding farmer families across India. A farmer family is defined as husband, wife, and minor children. No minimum or maximum land requirement. Exclusions (NOT eligible): 1. Institutional landholders (trusts, companies). 2. Former and present holders of constitutional posts (Ministers, MLAs, MPs, Mayors). 3. All serving or retired officers and employees of Central/State Government Ministries and their field units (except Multi-Tasking Staff/Class IV/Group D employees). 4. All persons who paid Income Tax in the last assessment year. 5. Professionals (registered doctors, engineers, lawyers, chartered accountants, architects) practicing their profession and earning monthly income > Rs 10,000. 6. All superannuated/retired pensioners with monthly pension > Rs 10,000 (excluding MTS/Class IV). Required documents: Aadhaar card (mandatory for DBT), bank account with IFSC code, land ownership records (7/12 extract in Maharashtra, Khasra/Khatauni in UP/MP), mobile number linked to Aadhaar. How to apply: 1. Online at pmkisan.gov.in — Self-registration or through Common Service Centre (CSC). 2. Through village-level Patwari/Revenue officer. 3. Through bank branch. Status check: pmkisan.gov.in/beneficiarystatus — enter Aadhaar or mobile number. Helpline: 155261 or 011-24300606 (Mon-Fri, 9:30 AM - 6:00 PM). Common issues: Name mismatch between Aadhaar and land records — get corrected at Tehsildar office. Bank account not linked to Aadhaar — visit bank for seeding.

source: PMFBY Operational Guidelines 2024 — Department of Agriculture & Cooperation
text: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) — comprehensive crop insurance for farmers. Premium rates (farmer's share): Kharif crops — 2% of sum insured. Rabi crops — 1.5% of sum insured. Annual commercial and horticultural crops — 5% of actuarial premium. Government pays the balance premium (often 15-25% of sum insured). Sum insured: Based on Scale of Finance (district-wise, crop-wise) decided by District Level Technical Committee (DLTC). Example: Wheat in Pune district — Sum Insured Rs 35,000/ha, farmer premium Rs 525/ha. Coverage: All food crops, oilseeds, annual commercial crops (cotton, sugarcane, jute), and horticultural crops (fruits, vegetables, spices). Risks covered: 1. Prevented sowing/planting (>75% area affected) — 25% of sum insured. 2. Standing crop losses due to drought, flood, hailstorm, cyclone, unseasonal rain, pest/disease. 3. Post-harvest losses — up to 14 days after harvest for crops left in 'cut and spread' condition. 4. Localized calamities — hailstorm, landslide, waterlogging (individual farm basis). 5. Add-on: Wild animal attack coverage (state option). Claim process: Report crop loss within 72 hours through: Crop Insurance App (available on Google Play), toll-free 1800-200-7710, nearest bank branch, Common Service Centre, or agriculture department office. Provide: Policy number, Aadhaar, crop photos showing damage, land records. Assessment: Crop Cutting Experiments (CCE) at village/GP level. Satellite remote sensing and drone surveys for faster assessment. Individual farm assessment for localized calamities. Enrolment: Kharif — April 1 to July 31. Rabi — October 1 to December 31. Loanee farmers — auto-enrolled through bank (opt-out by written declaration). Non-loanee farmers — voluntary, apply through bank/CSC/PMFBY portal. Since Kharif 2020, scheme is voluntary for all farmers. Maharashtra state insurance companies: Agriculture Insurance Company of India (AIC), HDFC ERGO, ICICI Lombard.

source: RBI & NABARD — Kisan Credit Card Scheme Guidelines
text: Kisan Credit Card (KCC) provides affordable crop loans to farmers. Interest rate: 7% per annum. With prompt repayment, 3% interest subvention — effective rate only 4% per annum. This is the cheapest institutional credit available to farmers. Credit limit: Up to Rs 3 lakh for crop production. Includes: Cost of cultivation, post-harvest expenses, farm maintenance, crop insurance premium (PMFBY auto-deducted). For animal husbandry and fisheries: Separate KCC with limit up to Rs 2 lakh. Limit calculation: Scale of Finance × Area cultivated + 10% towards post-harvest/maintenance + 20% towards crop insurance and contingencies. Limit is valid for 5 years with annual review. Eligibility: All farmers — owner cultivators, tenant farmers, sharecroppers, oral lessees, SHGs, JLGs. Both individual and joint holdings. No minimum land requirement. Required documents: Aadhaar card, PAN card (for limit > Rs 1 lakh), land records (7/12 extract, tenancy agreement), passport photo, bank account (will be opened if not existing). How to apply: Visit any commercial bank (SBI, PNB, Bank of India, etc.), cooperative bank, or Regional Rural Bank (RRB). Apply through PM-KISAN portal (option to apply for KCC). Saturation drive: Banks are mandated to issue KCC to all willing PM-KISAN beneficiaries. Processing time: Within 14 working days of complete application. No processing fee for limits up to Rs 3 lakh. Repayment: Within 12 months of each withdrawal. Flexible — withdraw and repay multiple times within limit. ATM-enabled KCC RuPay card issued for withdrawals. Important: If repayment delayed beyond 1 year, interest rate jumps to 7% (no subvention). If NPA (>90 days), rate becomes 12-14%. Always repay on time.

source: PM-KUSUM Official Guidelines — Ministry of New & Renewable Energy
text: Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthan Mahabhiyan (PM-KUSUM) promotes solar energy in agriculture. Three components: Component A — 10,000 MW grid-connected solar power plants on barren/fallow land. Farmers lease land and earn Rs 30,000-40,000/acre/year as rental income. Component B — Standalone solar agricultural pumps. 20 lakh individual pumps (up to 7.5 HP). Central subsidy: 30%, State subsidy: 30%, Farmer contribution: 40% (bank loan available). Example: 5 HP solar pump costs Rs 3-4 lakh. Farmer pays only Rs 1.2-1.6 lakh. No recurring electricity costs for 25 years. Component C — Solarisation of existing grid-connected pumps. Farmer installs solar panel on existing electric pump. Sells surplus power to DISCOM at Rs 3.5/unit. Earn Rs 50,000-80,000/year from surplus power sale. Central subsidy: 30%, State subsidy: 30%. Eligibility: All farmers with agricultural land. Priority to small and marginal farmers, SC/ST, women farmers. For Component B: Must have water source (borewell, open well, canal, river). No electricity connection at pump site. For Component C: Must have existing grid-connected pump with valid electricity connection. How to apply: Maharashtra — MEDA (Maharashtra Energy Development Agency) portal or mahadbt.maharashtra.gov.in. Other states — respective MNRE nodal agency. Required documents: Land records, Aadhaar, bank account, existing pump details (for Component C). Benefits: Zero electricity bill, excess power income, reliable irrigation (no power cuts), environmentally clean. Maintenance: Panels last 25 years, minimal maintenance. Clean panels monthly, check wiring annually.

source: Central Institute for Cotton Research (CICR), Nagpur — Best Practices for Maharashtra
text: Cotton cultivation best practices for Maharashtra (India's largest cotton-producing state): Varieties: Bt Cotton hybrids (Bollgard II) — 95% of area. Popular hybrids: Mahyco MRC-7361, Rasi RCH-659, JK Durga (JK-1050). Non-Bt: NHH-44, PKV-081, AKH-081 (for organic cultivation). Land preparation: Deep ploughing in May after harvest of rabi crop. 2-3 harrowing before sowing. Form ridges and furrows (for irrigated) or broad bed furrows (BBF for rainfed). Sowing: June 15 to July 15 (after receiving 100mm rainfall). Avoid sowing before June 15 (pink bollworm refuge period). Spacing: Rainfed — 90cm × 60cm (18,500 plants/ha). Irrigated — 120cm × 60cm (13,800 plants/ha). Seed rate: 2.0-2.5 kg/ha (4-5 packets of 450g). Nutrient management: Rainfed — 50:25:25 kg NPK/ha. Irrigated — 100:50:50 kg NPK/ha. Basal: Full P and K + 25% N at sowing. First top dress: 25% N at 30 days (square formation). Second top dress: 25% N at 60 days (flowering). Third top dress: 25% N at 90 days (boll development). Foliar spray: MgSO4 1% at flowering + KNO3 1% at boll development for better fiber quality. Water management: First irrigation at 21 days if no rain. Critical stages: Square formation (45 DAS), flowering (65 DAS), boll development (90 DAS). Avoid waterlogging — causes root rot. Pest management: Major pests — Pink bollworm (PBW), American bollworm (Helicoverpa), whitefly, sucking pests (jassid, aphid, thrips). PBW management: Mandatory — destroy crop residue by December 31. Install pheromone traps (5/ha) for monitoring. Spray Profenofos 50 EC + Emamectin benzoate 5 SG at ETL. Picking: Start when 60% bolls are open. Pick early morning after dew dries. Separate hand-picking (don't mix open and partially open). Grade as kapas (seed cotton). Marketing: Sell at CCI procurement centres at MSP (Rs 7,521/quintal medium staple, Rs 7,921/quintal long staple for 2025-26). Or through FPO/cooperative for potential premium. e-NAM auction for price discovery.

source: ICAR-IIWBR — Wheat Cultivation Guide for Central Zone (Maharashtra, MP, Gujarat)
text: Wheat cultivation comprehensive guide for central India: Varieties by sowing time: Timely sown (Nov 1-25): HD-2967 (most popular, high yield), GW-322 (irrigated), MACS-6222 (Maharashtra-specific), DBW-187 (new, rust resistant). Late sown (Dec 1-25): HD-3086 (heat tolerant), HI-1634, Raj-4037. Very late (after Dec 25): HD-3271, NW-1076 — avoid if possible, 20-30% yield loss. Land preparation: One deep ploughing + 2-3 harrowing. Laser leveling saves 20-25% irrigation water. Apply FYM 10-12 tonnes/ha 3-4 weeks before sowing. Seed rate: Timely — 100 kg/ha. Late — 125 kg/ha. Treat with Vitavax 75 WP (2.5g/kg) + Chlorpyrifos 20 EC (4ml/kg) + Trichoderma viride (4g/kg). Sowing method: Seed drill at 5-6 cm depth. Row spacing: 20-22.5 cm (irrigated timely), 15-18 cm (late sown). Nutrient management (irrigated): Timely — 120:60:40 kg NPK/ha. Late — 80:40:20 kg NPK/ha. Application: 1/2 N + full P + full K as basal. 1/4 N at first irrigation (CRI, 21 days). 1/4 N at second irrigation (tillering, 40-45 days). Zinc sulphate 25 kg/ha if soil Zn < 0.6 ppm. Irrigation schedule (5-6 irrigations for full potential): CRI (Crown Root Initiation) — 18-21 DAS (most critical, never miss). Tillering — 38-42 DAS. Late jointing — 58-62 DAS. Flowering — 78-82 DAS. Milking — 98-102 DAS. Dough — 112-115 DAS (skip if water scarce). If limited water (3 irrigations only): CRI + flowering + milking — gets 80% of full yield. Weed control: Pre-emergence — Pendimethalin 30 EC (1.0 kg/ha) within 2-3 days of sowing. Post-emergence — Sulfosulfuron 75 WG (25g/ha) at 25-30 DAS for Phalaris minor. 2,4-D sodium salt (0.5 kg/ha) for broadleaf weeds at 30-35 DAS. Harvest: When grain turns golden, hard and dry (moisture <20%). Combine harvester saves time and reduces losses to 2-3% vs 5-8% manual. Yield potential: Irrigated timely — 45-55 quintals/ha. Rainfed — 25-30 quintals/ha. Late sown irrigated — 30-40 quintals/ha. MSP 2025-26: Rs 2,425 per quintal. Sell through APMC mandi or e-NAM for transparent auction.

source: ICAR-IISR Indore — Soybean Production Technology for Maharashtra
text: Soybean — Maharashtra is India's largest producer (Vidarbha, Marathwada, Western Maharashtra regions). Varieties: JS-9560 (most popular, early maturing, 88-93 days), JS-2034 (Vidarbha-specific, high yield), MACS-1407 (Maharashtra Agricultural), KDS-726 (waterlogging tolerant), NRC-142 (new, high oil content). Land preparation: Deep summer ploughing in May. 2 harrowing + planking for fine seedbed. Broad Bed Furrow (BBF) method recommended — prevents waterlogging. Sowing: June 20 to July 10 after receiving 100mm cumulative rainfall. NEVER sow dry. Delay beyond July 15 reduces yield by 40-50 kg/ha per day. Seed rate: 65-75 kg/ha. Use fresh certified seed — germination drops fast if stored beyond 8 months. Seed treatment: Thiram 2g + Carbendazim 1g per kg seed (against seed-borne diseases). Then Rhizobium japonicum + PSB (Phosphate Solubilizing Bacteria) inoculation in shade, air dry 30 min before sowing. Row spacing: 30-45 cm. Plant spacing: 5-7 cm. Nutrient management: 30:60:30:20 kg N:P₂O₅:K₂O:S per ha as basal at sowing. No nitrogen top dressing needed — soybean fixes 80-100 kg N/ha through Rhizobium. Sulphur is critical — deficiency common in Maharashtra soils. Weed management: Most critical during first 30 days. Pre-emergence: Pendimethalin 30 EC (1.0 kg/ha) within 2 DAS. Post-emergence: Imazethapyr 10 SL (75 ml/ha) at 15-20 DAS for grassy and broadleaf weeds. One hand weeding at 25-30 DAS for clean fields. Key pests: 1. Stem fly (Melanagromyza sojae) — seed treatment with Thiamethoxam 30 FS (10ml/kg). 2. Girdle beetle (Obereopsis brevis) — most destructive. ETL: 3 grubs per meter row. Spray Profenofos 50 EC (1.5ml/L) or Lambda-cyhalothrin 5 EC (0.6ml/L) at pod formation. 3. Tobacco caterpillar (Spodoptera litura) — use NPV 250 LE/ha or Chlorantraniliprole 18.5 SC (0.3ml/L). Diseases: Rust (Phakopsora pachyrhizi) — spray Hexaconazole 5 EC (2ml/L) at first appearance. Harvest: When 95% pods turn brown, leaves shed, stems dry. Grain moisture <13%. Use sickle or combine (with soybean header). Avoid delay — pod shattering losses increase rapidly. Yield: 20-25 quintals/ha (irrigated), 12-18 quintals/ha (rainfed). MSP 2025-26: Rs 4,892 per quintal.

source: Vasantdada Sugar Institute (VSI) Pune & ICAR-SBI — Sugarcane Production Technology
text: Sugarcane cultivation guide for Maharashtra (India's 2nd largest producer): Varieties: Popular in Maharashtra — Co-86032 (most widely planted), CoM-0265 (early maturing), CoVSI-9805 (high sugar), MS-10001 (new, high yield). Planting: Adsali (July-August) — 16-18 month crop, highest yield 120-150 tonnes/ha. Pre-seasonal (October-November) — 14-15 month. Suru (January-February) — 12 month, 80-100 tonnes/ha. Seed rate: 3-bud setts, 30,000-35,000 setts/ha (7-8 tonnes seed cane). Treat setts with Carbendazim 2g/L for 15 minutes (against smut, wilt). Spacing: 120-150 cm (single row), 90 cm (paired row with 180 cm gap — better for mechanization and intercropping). Nutrient management: 250:115:115 kg NPK/ha for Adsali. 200:85:85 for Suru. Apply in 3-4 splits. Use farmyard manure 20-25 tonnes/ha. Pressmud (filter cake) 10 tonnes/ha — excellent organic amendment. Irrigation: Most water-intensive crop (1500-2000 mm). Drip irrigation saves 40-50% water with 15-20% yield increase. Critical periods: Germination (4-6 weeks), tillering (6-12 weeks), grand growth (July-September for Adsali). Skip irrigation 3 weeks before harvest for better sugar recovery. Intercropping: Short-duration crops in initial 3-4 months — onion, soybean, groundnut, vegetables. Earn Rs 20,000-40,000/ha additional income. Harvest: Manual or mechanical (harvester available through sugar factory). Harvest when sugar content > 10.5% (measure with hand refractometer). Deliver to factory within 24 hours (sugar loss 0.02% per hour delay). Payment: Fair & Remunerative Price (FRP) — Rs 3,150/quintal (at 10.25% recovery). Additional: Maharashtra State Advised Price (SAP) — typically Rs 300-500/quintal above FRP. Revenue sharing formula: 75% to farmers, 25% to sugar factory.

source: ICAR-DOGR Pune — Onion Production Technology for Maharashtra
text: Onion cultivation in Maharashtra (Nashik, Pune, Ahmednagar — India's onion bowl): Seasons: Kharif (June-July planting, October harvest) — higher risk, higher price. Late Kharif (August-September, January harvest) — moderate. Rabi (November-December, April-May harvest) — highest production, best storage. Varieties: Rabi — N-2-4-1 (Nashik selection, best for storage), Bhima Kiran, Bhima Shakti. Kharif — Bhima Super, Agrifound Dark Red, NHRDF Red. Nursery: Raise seedlings for 6-8 weeks. Seed rate: 8-10 kg/ha. Treat with Thiram 2g/kg. Transplant at 4-6 leaf stage (pencil thickness). Spacing: 15cm × 10cm on flat beds or raised beds. Plant density: 6-7 lakh plants/ha. Nutrient management: 110:40:60 kg NPK/ha. Sulphur 30 kg/ha (critical for pungency and storage). Basal: 50% N + full P + full K + full S. Top dress: 25% N at 30 DAT, 25% N at 45 DAT. Stop nitrogen 60 days before harvest — excess N reduces storage life. Irrigation: Critical at transplanting (daily for 7 days), bulb initiation (45-55 DAT), bulb development (65-85 DAT). Stop irrigation 10-15 days before harvest for better curing and storage. Total water requirement: 500-600mm. Disease management: Purple blotch (Alternaria porri) — most important. Spray Mancozeb 75 WP (2.5g/L) alternating with Difenconazole 25 EC (1ml/L) every 10-12 days. Stemphylium blight — spray Chlorothalonil 75 WP. Basal rot (Fusarium) — soil drench Carbendazim, avoid waterlogging. Thrips (Thrips tabaci) — major pest. Spray Fipronil 5 SC (1.5ml/L) or Spinetoram 11.7 SC (0.5ml/L). Use blue sticky traps. Harvest and storage: Harvest when 50-75% tops fall and neck becomes thin. Cure in field for 3-5 days. Grade into A (>55mm), B (35-55mm), C (<35mm). Storage: Well-ventilated bottom-ventilated onion storage structure. Storage losses: 25-30% over 4-5 months (sprout, rot, weight loss). Use maleic hydrazide spray 15 days before harvest to reduce sprouting. Market: APMC mandi (Lasalgaon — Asia's largest onion market). NCEL (National Commodity Exchange) for futures. Price volatility: Rs 500-10,000/quintal depending on supply.

source: Ministry of Agriculture — Compiled Major Scheme Directory 2025-26
text: Comprehensive guide to major government schemes for Indian farmers (2025-26): 1. PM-KISAN (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi): Rs 6,000/year direct transfer in 3 instalments. All landholding families. Portal: pmkisan.gov.in. 2. PMFBY (Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana): Crop insurance. Kharif 2% premium, Rabi 1.5%. Claims via app or 1800-200-7710. Voluntary since 2020. 3. KCC (Kisan Credit Card): Crop loan at 4% effective interest (with subvention). Up to Rs 3 lakh. Apply at any bank. 4. PM-KUSUM: Solar pumps 60% subsidy (30% central + 30% state). Solarize grid pumps, earn from surplus power. 5. PMKSY-PDMC (Per Drop More Crop): Micro-irrigation subsidy 55% general, 70% SC/ST and small farmers. Drip and sprinkler systems. 6. Soil Health Card: Free soil testing every 2 years. Nutrient-wise recommendations. Apply at KVK or state soil lab. 7. e-NAM (National Agriculture Market): Online trading across 1,361 mandis. Transparent price discovery. Register at enam.gov.in with Aadhaar + bank account. 8. NFSM (National Food Security Mission): Free/subsidized seeds, equipment, and demonstrations for wheat, rice, pulses, oilseeds, nutri-cereals. Apply through district agriculture officer. 9. RKVY-RAFTAAR: State-level flexible funding for agriculture and allied sectors. Includes agri-entrepreneurship with up to Rs 25 lakh grant. 10. MIDH (Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture): Subsidy for fruit orchards (Rs 30,000-60,000/ha), protected cultivation (50% subsidy on polyhouse/shade net), post-harvest infrastructure. Maharashtra-specific portals: MahaDBT (mahadbt.maharashtra.gov.in) — single window for 40+ agricultural subsidies. Nanaji Deshmukh Krishi Sanjivani Prakalp (PoCRA) — Rs 4,000 crore World Bank-funded project for drought-prone districts.

source: e-NAM Portal — National Agriculture Market
text: e-NAM (National Agriculture Market) is an electronic trading portal linking 1,361 APMC mandis across India. How it works: Farmer brings produce to e-NAM registered mandi → Gate entry with lot details → Quality assaying (moisture, foreign matter, broken) → Lot displayed online → Traders across all connected mandis bid electronically → Highest bid wins → Payment through e-NAM account within 24-48 hours. Registration: Free. Visit nearest e-NAM mandi or register online at enam.gov.in. Required: Aadhaar, bank account, mobile number. Farmer gets: Unique registration number + e-NAM trading account. Benefits for farmers: 1. Better price discovery — bids from multiple traders across states, not just local. Average 5-15% higher price realization. 2. Transparent weighing and quality testing at mandi gate. 3. Electronic payment — no cash delays, no middle-man deduction. 4. Real-time price information across all connected mandis. 5. Reduced market fee — some states have reduced/unified APMC charges for e-NAM. Maharashtra e-NAM mandis: Over 120 mandis integrated including Nashik, Pune, Nagpur, Ahmednagar, Solapur, Kolhapur. Key commodities: Onion (Lasalgaon, Pune), Soybean (Latur, Nanded), Cotton (Jalgaon, Amravati), Wheat (Nagpur). How to check prices: e-NAM mobile app (Android/iOS) or website enam.gov.in/web/dashboard/trade-data. Shows: Commodity, mandi, date, modal price, arrivals (in quintals). FPO (Farmer Producer Organization) integration: FPOs can aggregate and sell on e-NAM. Reduces per-farmer transport cost. Collective bargaining power. Government provides Rs 15 lakh/FPO for equity grant + Rs 18 lakh for credit guarantee.

source: SFAC & NABARD — Farmer Producer Organization Guidelines
text: Farmer Producer Organizations (FPOs) — collective farming and marketing for smallholders. What is an FPO: A registered body of farmers (minimum 300 in plains, 100 in hilly/tribal areas) organized as a Producer Company under Companies Act or a cooperative society. Purpose: Collective input purchase (seeds, fertilizer at wholesale), shared equipment, collective marketing (better prices), value addition, and market access. Government support under 10,000 FPO Formation Scheme: 1. Equity grant: Up to Rs 15 lakh per FPO (Rs 2,000/member, max Rs 15 lakh) to build share capital. 2. Credit Guarantee: Rs 2 crore per FPO through Credit Guarantee Fund — enables bank loans without collateral. 3. Management cost: Rs 18 lakh over 3 years for hiring CEO, accountant, and operational expenses. 4. Cluster-Based Business Organization (CBBO): Mentoring and handholding agency assigned to each FPO for 5 years. How to form: Gather 300+ farmers in a district. Choose implementing agency (NABARD, SFAC, state agency). Register as Producer Company with RoC. Open bank account, hire CEO. Develop business plan. Success stories from Maharashtra: Sahyadri Farms (Nashik) — India's largest FPO, 15,000+ farmers, exports grapes and pomegranates to Europe. Annual turnover Rs 800+ crore. Abhinav Farmers Club (Pune) — 2,000 farmers, organic vegetables to metro cities. Benefits: 10-20% reduction in input costs through bulk purchase. 15-30% higher produce prices through direct institutional/retail supply. Access to processing and cold storage infrastructure. Direct export opportunities.

source: ICAR-CSSRI — Crop Residue Management and Conservation Agriculture
text: Crop residue management — alternatives to stubble burning: Why not to burn: Rs 15,000/ha penalty under Air Quality Management Commission order. Destroys soil organic carbon, kills beneficial organisms, causes air pollution. Loses 25% nitrogen, 50% sulphur, 25% phosphorus from soil. Alternatives: 1. Happy Seeder: Sow wheat directly into rice stubble. No need to clear residue. Saves Rs 5,000-6,000/ha on land preparation. 80% subsidy available under CRM Scheme. 2. Mulching: Leave residue as surface cover — retains moisture, suppresses weeds, adds organic matter. Use rotavator to chop residue, then sow with zero-till drill. 3. Composting: Collect residue, treat with Waste Decomposer (NCOF) — 4 bottles (Rs 20 each) decompose 1 tonne residue in 30-40 days. Mix with FYM for premium compost. 4. Baling: Bale straw for animal feed, mushroom cultivation, or biomass power plants. Income: Rs 2,000-3,000/tonne for rice straw bales. 5. Biochar: Pyrolyze residue into biochar — excellent soil amendment. Improves water retention, CEC, and carbon sequestration. Conservation Agriculture principles: Minimum soil disturbance (zero-till/minimum till), permanent soil cover (residue/mulch/cover crops), crop diversification (rotate cereals with legumes). Benefits: 15-20% reduction in input costs, improved soil health over 3-5 years, better water infiltration, 10-15% higher yield in drought years.

source: NDDB & ICAR-NDRI — Dairy Farming as Supplementary Income
text: Integrated dairy farming for crop farmers — supplementary income and nutrient cycling: Breed selection for Maharashtra: Gir, Sahiwal (indigenous), Holstein-Friesian × Sahiwal cross (HF cross), Murrah buffalo. HF cross gives 12-18 litres/day, indigenous breeds 6-10 litres/day. Murrah buffalo: 8-12 litres/day with 7%+ fat. Economics (2 HF cross cows): Investment — Rs 1.5 lakh (cattle) + Rs 50,000 (shed). Income — 25-30 litres/day × Rs 35-40/litre = Rs 900-1,200/day. Feed cost — Rs 300-400/day. Net income: Rs 500-800/day = Rs 15,000-24,000/month from 2 cows. Plus: 15-20 tonnes of dung/year (worth Rs 15,000-20,000 as FYM/vermicompost). Schemes: 1. National Livestock Mission (NLM): 50% subsidy on purchase of breeding animals. 2. Dairy Entrepreneurship Development Scheme (DEDS): 33.33% subsidy (25% for general, 33.33% for SC/ST/women). For dairy units of 2-10 animals. Max subsidy Rs 7 lakh. 3. NABARD dairy loan: At 10-12% interest, with subsidy component. 4. KCC for dairy: Rs 1.6 lakh limit per animal (cow) or Rs 2 lakh (buffalo). Marketing: Sell through cooperative (Gokul, Mahananda, Amul) for assured procurement. Or direct to local consumers at higher price (Rs 50-60/litre in cities). Value addition: Paneer (Rs 300-350/kg), ghee (Rs 500-700/kg), curd (Rs 50-80/kg).

source: ICAR-CIPHET & FCI — Post-Harvest Management for Food Grains
text: Post-harvest management to reduce losses (India loses Rs 90,000 crore/year in post-harvest wastage): Drying: Reduce grain moisture to safe storage level — Wheat <12%, Rice <14%, Pulses <10%, Oilseeds <8%. Solar drying on clean platform (tarpaulin/concrete floor). Mechanical dryer for rainy season harvest (Rs 2-5 lakh, 50% subsidy under SMAM). Cleaning and grading: Remove chaff, broken grains, stones, weed seeds. Use manual sieves or mechanical cleaner-grader. Grading increases price by Rs 100-500/quintal. Storage: Safe storage options by scale — Small farmer (up to 50 quintals): Metal bins (Rs 5,000-15,000, 50% subsidy), Pusa bin (polythene-lined, airtight), improved kothi. Medium (50-500 quintals): CAP storage (Cover and Plinth), warehouse receipt from nearest warehouse. Large/FPO: Godown construction (50% subsidy under SMAM/AMI scheme, up to Rs 15 lakh). Hermetic storage: Hermetic (airtight) bags — GrainPro, PIC bags. No need for chemical fumigation. Pest control in storage: Use aluminium phosphide tablets (3g/tonne) — ONLY by trained personnel (highly toxic). Neem leaf powder layering — 2-3% by weight (traditional, safe). Deltamethrin 2.5 WP — spray on bag surface. Warehouse receipt financing: Store grain in WDRA-registered warehouse, get receipt, pledge at bank for up to 70% of value as loan. Sell when prices are better. Interest: 7-9%/year.

source: ICAR-NICRA — Climate Resilient Agriculture Practices
text: Climate-smart agriculture practices for Maharashtra (drought-prone Marathwada and Vidarbha): Drought management: 1. Short-duration varieties — mature 10-15 days earlier, escape terminal drought. Soybean: JS-9560 (88 days), Wheat: HD-3086 (110 days). 2. Protective irrigation at critical stages — even 1 supplemental irrigation during flowering can save 50% yield in drought. Use stored rainwater from farm pond. 3. Seed priming — soak seeds in 1% KCl or 2% DAP solution for 12-16 hours, dry back. Improves germination vigor by 15-20% under moisture stress. 4. Anti-transpirant spray — Kaolin 6% spray reduces water loss through leaves. Mulching reduces soil evaporation. Flood resilience: 1. Raised bed planting — 15-20cm raised beds prevent waterlogging for soybean, pulses. 2. Quick-drainage varieties — KDS-726 soybean tolerates 5-7 days waterlogging. 3. Contingency crop plans — if kharif crop fails by August 15, sow short-duration millets (bajra 60-70 days, proso millet 60 days) as catch crop. Heat stress: 1. Early sowing — finish wheat sowing by November 25 to avoid March heat during grain filling. 2. Light irrigation during heat waves reduces canopy temperature by 3-5°C. 3. Foliar spray of KNO3 (1%) or ZnSO4 (0.5%) during grain filling under heat stress. Carbon sequestration opportunities: Agroforestry (subabul, teak border planting) — earn carbon credits + timber income. Biochar application — sequesters carbon for 100+ years. Soil organic carbon improvement through residue management, green manuring.

source: ICAR-IIMR (Indian Institute of Millets Research) — Jowar Production Technology
text: Jowar (Sorghum) cultivation for Maharashtra — traditional crop well-suited for rainfed conditions: Varieties: Kharif — CSH-14 (hybrid, grain), CSV-20 (dual-purpose grain+fodder), CSH-16 (high yield). Rabi — Maldandi (M35-1, most popular in Maharashtra for roti/bhakri), CSV-22R, Phule Vasudha, SPV-2217. Rabi jowar is unique to Maharashtra/Karnataka — grown on residual soil moisture after monsoon. Sowing: Kharif — June-July with monsoon onset. Rabi — September 15 to October 15 (on stored soil moisture). Late sowing reduces yield significantly. Seed rate: 7-10 kg/ha (hybrids), 10-12 kg/ha (varieties). Spacing: Kharif — 45cm × 15cm. Rabi — 45cm × 12cm. Nutrient management: Kharif — 80:40:40 kg NPK/ha. Rabi — 50:25:25 kg NPK/ha (lower due to moisture limitation). FYM 5-8 tonnes/ha. Special for Rabi: Apply full fertilizer at sowing — no top dressing (can't irrigate). Water management: Kharif — rainfed, drainage important. Rabi — grown entirely on stored soil moisture (unique). Deep black soils with 150cm+ depth retain enough moisture for full rabi crop. If protective irrigation available (1-2 irrigations), yield increases 50-80%. Key pests: Shoot fly (Atherigona soccata) — most damaging. Early sowing escapes peak fly period. Seed treatment Imidacloprid 48 FS (12ml/kg). Stem borer — Carbofuran 3G (8kg/ha) in leaf whorl. Harvest: Kharif — October-November. Rabi — February-March. Cut ear heads when grain is hard. Thresh manually or mechanically. Yield: Kharif hybrid — 30-40 quintals/ha. Rabi — 15-25 quintals/ha (Maldandi). MSP 2025-26: Jowar (Hybrid) Rs 3,371/quintal, Jowar (Maldandi) Rs 3,421/quintal. Dual income: Grain + fodder (20-25 tonnes green fodder/ha). Excellent for dairy farmers.

source: ICAR-IIPR — Gram (Chickpea) Production Technology for Central India
text: Gram (Bengal gram/Chickpea) — India's most important pulse crop, Maharashtra is a major producer: Varieties: Desi type — JAKI-9218 (wilt resistant, most popular in Maharashtra), Vijay, Digvijay, Phule Vikram. Kabuli type — KAK-2 (large seeded, premium price), Kripa, MNK-1. Sowing: October 15 to November 15 (Rabi season). Sow on residual soil moisture after kharif harvest. Late sowing — use short duration varieties like JG-14. Seed rate: Desi — 80-100 kg/ha. Kabuli — 100-120 kg/ha (larger seed size). Seed treatment: Vitavax 75 WP (2g/kg) + Trichoderma viride (4g/kg) + Rhizobium + PSB inoculation. Spacing: 30cm × 10cm. Nutrient management: 20:40:20 kg NPK/ha as basal only. Gram is a nitrogen-fixing legume — adds 40-60 kg N/ha to soil for next crop. Rhizobium inoculation critical if field is being sown with gram for first time. Sulphur 20 kg/ha improves protein content. Weed management: Pendimethalin 30 EC (1.0 kg/ha) pre-emergence. One hand weeding at 30-35 DAS. Irrigation: Mostly rainfed on stored moisture. If available: 1 irrigation at branching (30 DAS) + 1 at pod filling (55 DAS). Over-irrigation harmful — causes excessive vegetative growth and reduces pod setting. Critical disease: Fusarium wilt — most serious. Use resistant varieties (JAKI-9218, JG-62). Seed treatment with Trichoderma. Avoid fields with wilt history for 3 years. Ascochyta blight — spray Mancozeb (2.5g/L) at first symptom. Pod borer (Helicoverpa armigera): ETL: 1 larva per meter row. NPV 250 LE/ha at 50% flowering. Spray Spinosad 45 SC (0.2ml/L) if severe. Pheromone traps (5/ha) for monitoring. Bird perches (20/ha) attract predatory birds. Harvest: When pods turn brown and plant dries. Don't delay — pod shattering. Yield: 15-20 quintals/ha (irrigated), 8-12 quintals/ha (rainfed). MSP 2025-26: Rs 5,650/quintal (Desi), Kabuli fetches Rs 7,000-9,000/quintal in open market.

source: ICAR-IIVR & NHB — Vegetable Cultivation for Smallholders
text: High-value vegetable farming for smallholder farmers in Maharashtra: Most profitable vegetables by season: Rabi (Oct-Feb): Tomato (Rs 60,000-1,00,000/ha net), Cauliflower (Rs 50,000-80,000/ha), Capsicum (Rs 80,000-1,20,000/ha in polyhouse). Summer (Feb-May): Watermelon (Rs 40,000-70,000/ha), Cucumber, Bitter gourd. Kharif (Jun-Sep): Bhindi/Okra (Rs 30,000-50,000/ha), Chilli (Rs 1,00,000-2,00,000/ha for dry chilli). Year-round in polyhouse: Capsicum, Tomato, Cucumber — income Rs 3-5 lakh/1000 sq.m/year. Protected cultivation: Low-cost polyhouse (200 gauge UV film): Rs 500-700/sq.m. NHB subsidy: 50% up to Rs 56 lakh per 4000 sq.m. Shade net house: Rs 350-500/sq.m, 50% subsidy. Ideal for leafy vegetables, flowers, nursery. Drip + mulch + fertigation combination increases vegetable yield by 40-60%. Key practices: 1. Raised bed nursery with coco peat + vermicompost (1:1). Transplant strong seedlings for better establishment. 2. Staking for tomato, capsicum, cucumber — improves quality and reduces disease. 3. Plastic mulch: Black for soil warming, silver for pest repellence. 4. Fertigation: Weekly schedule with water-soluble fertilizers through drip. 5. IPM: Yellow sticky traps for whitefly/thrips, pheromone traps for fruit borer, Trichoderma soil drench for wilt. Marketing: Direct to APMC mandi, local markets, retail chains (Reliance Fresh, Big Bazaar), hotel/restaurant supply. FPO aggregation for consistent supply. Contract farming with companies. Cold chain: Mini cold storage (5-10 MT) with subsidy under MIDH. Extends shelf life of vegetables from 2-3 days to 15-20 days.

source: Maharashtra Government — MahaDBT Agricultural Schemes Portal
text: MahaDBT (Maharashtra Direct Benefit Transfer) — single window for 40+ agricultural subsidies: Portal: mahadbt.maharashtra.gov.in. Registration: Aadhaar-based. One-time registration, apply for multiple schemes. Major agricultural schemes on MahaDBT: 1. Micro-irrigation (Drip/Sprinkler): 55-70% subsidy. Max Rs 80,000/ha for drip, Rs 30,000/ha for sprinkler. 2. Farm Mechanization: 40-50% subsidy on tractors, power tillers, implements. Max Rs 1.25 lakh for tractor (small farmer), Rs 75,000 for power tiller. 3. Protected cultivation: Polyhouse 50% (up to Rs 56 lakh/4000 sq.m), shade net 50% (up to Rs 18 lakh/4000 sq.m). 4. Fruit crop planting: Mango Rs 30,000/ha, Pomegranate Rs 30,000/ha, Grapes Rs 60,000/ha subsidy for new orchards. 5. Post-harvest: Cold storage, warehouse, processing unit subsidies. Pack house Rs 4 lakh subsidy. 6. Watershed development: Farm pond Rs 50,000, percolation tank, nala bunding under Jalyukt Shivar / Magel Tyala Shet Tale. 7. Cattle purchase: 50% subsidy on crossbred cow/buffalo (max Rs 50,000). 8. Poultry/Goatery: 50% subsidy on backyard poultry (100 birds), goat unit (10+1). How to apply: 1. Register on mahadbt.maharashtra.gov.in with Aadhaar + mobile. 2. Complete farmer profile (land details from 7/12 extract). 3. Select scheme, upload required documents (7/12, 8A, Aadhaar, bank passbook, caste certificate if applicable). 4. Application goes through Taluka Agriculture Officer → District Superintendent Agriculture Officer → Approval. 5. Subsidy credited directly to bank account after verification. Tips: Apply early in financial year (April) — funds are limited and first-come-first-serve. Keep 7/12 extract updated with current crop details. Link Aadhaar to bank account for DBT.

source: ICAR-NRC Pomegranate Solapur — Pomegranate Production Technology
text: Pomegranate cultivation for Maharashtra (India's largest producer — Solapur, Nashik, Sangli, Ahmednagar): Varieties: Bhagwa (most popular, dark red aril, export quality), Arakta, Mridula, Ganesh (traditional). Bhagwa commands Rs 60-120/kg in domestic market, Rs 150-250/kg for export. Planting: Spacing 4.5m × 3m (740 plants/ha) for commercial orchards. Pit size: 60cm × 60cm × 60cm. Fill with 20kg FYM + 1kg SSP + 50g Trichoderma. Season: June-July (monsoon) or February-March. Bahar treatment (flowering regulation): Unique to pomegranate. Three bahars: Ambe bahar (Jan-Feb flowering, June-Aug harvest), Mrig bahar (June-July flowering, Nov-Jan harvest — most popular), Hasta bahar (Sept-Oct flowering, Feb-Mar harvest). Stress the tree by withholding water + applying Ethrel 3ml/L to induce leaf fall → rest period → resume irrigation + fertilization → synchronized flowering. Nutrition: 500:250:250 g NPK per tree per year (bearing tree). Apply in 3 splits. Foliar spray: ZnSO4 0.5% + Borax 0.3% at flowering. Micronutrient deficiency common — Fe, Zn, B. Major diseases: 1. Bacterial blight (Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. punicae) — most devastating. Causes oily spots on leaves/fruit, fruit cracking. Spray Streptocycline 500 ppm + Copper hydroxide 2g/L. Avoid overhead irrigation. Remove and destroy infected fruits. 2. Wilt (Ceratocystis fimbriata) — fatal, no cure. Remove and burn infected trees. Solarize soil. Plant on raised beds for drainage. 3. Fruit rot — spray Carbendazim at fruit set. Pests: Fruit borer (Deudorix isocrates) — spray Emamectin benzoate 5 SG at fruit set. Bag individual fruits with butter paper bags for export quality. Yield: 10-15 tonnes/ha from 4th year. Peak bearing at 8-12 years. Orchard life: 25-30 years. Economics: Establishment cost Rs 3-4 lakh/ha. Annual maintenance Rs 1.5-2 lakh/ha. Gross income Rs 4-8 lakh/ha. Net profit Rs 2-5 lakh/ha. Export: NRC Pomegranate provides export guidance. Register with APEDA for phytosanitary certificate. EU, UAE, and Southeast Asia are major markets.

source: NABARD & RBI — Agricultural Finance and Credit for Farmers
text: Agricultural finance options for Indian farmers: 1. Crop Loans (Short-term): Through KCC at 4% effective interest (7% - 3% subvention for prompt repayment). Up to Rs 3 lakh. 12-month tenure. No collateral needed up to Rs 1.6 lakh. 2. Term Loans (Medium/Long-term): For farm development — irrigation, land leveling, orchard establishment, farm equipment. Interest: 8.5-12%. Tenure: 3-7 years. Subsidy component under various government schemes reduces effective cost. 3. SHG-Bank Linkage: Women's Self-Help Group borrows at 7% interest. With government subsidy, effective rate can be 0-4%. Suitable for small loans (Rs 50,000-5 lakh per SHG). 4. Microfinance/MFI: Quick disbursement but higher interest (18-26%). Use only for urgent short-term needs. 5. Agri-Gold Loans: Pledge gold for agricultural loan at 7% interest (with subvention). SBI, PNB, cooperative banks. Quick processing (same day). 6. Warehouse Receipt Finance: Store produce in WDRA warehouse, get receipt, pledge for 70% value loan at 7-9%. Sell when prices rise. Perfect for onion, soybean, gram farmers. Government interest subvention: 2% subvention on crop loans up to Rs 3 lakh. Additional 3% prompt repayment incentive. Effective rate: 4% (cheapest institutional credit). Extended to: KCC holders, dairy, fishery, poultry farmers. Credit score improvement tips for farmers: Maintain savings account with regular transactions. Repay all loans on time (most important factor). Keep land records updated. Insurance coverage (PMFBY) improves creditworthiness. Digital transactions through UPI/bank.

source: ICAR-CAFRI — Agroforestry for Sustainable Income
text: Agroforestry — integrating trees with crops for multiple income streams and environmental benefits: Models for Maharashtra: 1. Boundary planting: Teak, subabul (Leucaena), neem on farm boundaries. 5-10% area, doesn't reduce crop area. Teak: Rs 15,000-25,000 per tree at 15-20 years. 200 boundary trees = Rs 30-50 lakh at maturity. 2. Agri-silviculture: Teak/Sagwan (6m × 6m) with soybean/wheat between rows for first 5-6 years. Switch to shade-tolerant crops (turmeric, ginger) as canopy closes. 3. Agri-horticulture: Mango/Pomegranate (6m × 6m or 5m × 3m) with intercrops. Fruit income from year 4-5 onwards + crop income annually. 4. Silvi-pasture: Subabul + grass (Napier/guinea grass) for dairy farmers. Subabul fodder (22% protein) + grass for roughage. 5. Poplar-based (for north India): 5m × 4m spacing, harvest at 7-8 years. Rs 3,000-5,000 per tree for plywood industry. Government support: Sub-Mission on Agroforestry (SMAF) — Rs 25,000/ha subsidy for tree planting on farmland. MGNREGA — 100 days wage for tree planting on own land (horticulture/forestry works). State nurseries provide subsidized saplings. Carbon credit potential: Agroforestry sequesters 5-10 tonnes CO2 per hectare per year. Carbon credit markets emerging — Rs 500-2,000 per tonne CO2. Timber regulations in Maharashtra: Transit permit required for cutting and transporting timber (except certain exempted species). Plant species not requiring felling permission: Subabul, Eucalyptus, Casuarina, poplar. Register on Mahaforest portal for hassle-free transit.

source: ICAR-DMR Solan — Mushroom Cultivation for Extra Income
text: Mushroom cultivation — ideal supplementary income for farmers with crop residue: Types suitable for Maharashtra: 1. Oyster mushroom (Pleurotus species): Easiest to grow. Temperature: 20-30°C. Grow year-round in shade/polyhouse. Substrate: Paddy straw, wheat straw, cotton waste. Investment: Rs 10,000-25,000 for 100 bag unit. Revenue: Rs 15,000-30,000/month. 2. Button mushroom (Agaricus bisporus): Premium price. Temperature: 14-18°C (requires AC or only winter season in Maharashtra). Substrate: Compost from wheat straw + chicken manure. Higher investment but Rs 200-250/kg retail. 3. Milky mushroom (Calocybe indica): Best for tropical climate. Temperature: 25-35°C. Substrate: Paddy straw. Growing period: 30-45 days. Step-by-step for Oyster mushroom: 1. Prepare substrate: Chop straw to 2-3 inches, soak in hot water (80°C) for 1 hour (pasteurization). Drain, cool to room temperature. 2. Spawning: Layer substrate and spawn (grain spawn, Rs 40-60/kg) in polythene bags (60×40 cm). Rate: 2-3% spawn by wet weight. Make 10-12 holes in bag. 3. Incubation: Keep in dark room at 25-28°C for 15-20 days. White mycelium covers entire bag. 4. Fruiting: Move to well-ventilated room with indirect light. Maintain 80-85% humidity (spray water 2-3 times/day). Temperature 20-28°C. 5. Harvest: Pin heads appear in 3-4 days. Harvest in 2-3 more days when caps are 5-8 cm. Twist and pull gently. 3-4 flushes possible from one bag. Yield: 700-800g per kg dry substrate. Economics per 500 bags/batch: Cost Rs 30,000 (substrate, spawn, bags, water). Revenue Rs 70,000-90,000 (at Rs 150-200/kg). Profit: Rs 40,000-60,000 per batch (45-60 days). Marketing: Local markets, hotels, restaurants, online (BigBasket, Amazon Fresh). Dry mushroom (Rs 800-1,200/kg) for longer shelf life.
